entries.title: The Empty Pantry and the Abstract Right
entries.text:
30 December 2026, 12:08. Home, Tughlak Road.

I have sat down to write, but the paper is silent and the room is louder. The silence is not the peaceful quiet of a study in Berlin, where the only sound is the scratch of the nib or the distant murmur of the street. It is the silence of a void. The cupboard is empty. The stove is cold. I have not eaten since yesterday morning. The body, which I have often treated as a mere vessel for the spirit, has now become the dominant voice in the house. It does not argue; it simply is. It is a fact, as stubborn and undeniable as gravity.

I look at my pocket. One hundred and six rupees. This is the concrete limit of my will. It is a number, like the reference number DE/2026/114, but this one does not bind me to a file; it binds me to hunger. The Directorate of Estates has taken my state funds, leaving me with this pittance, and the identity query remains unanswered. I am G. Hegel, the philosopher, but I am also a man who cannot buy a loaf of bread. The abstract right to sustenance, which I have expounded in my lectures, has no purchase here. It is a ghost in the machine of my daily life.

The plan for the afternoon was to visit the grocer, to buy food, to pay Ramesh. But the plan is a phantom. It exists only in the mind, in the realm of intention. It has not been sublated into reality. The heat of the day is not an obstacle; the lack of cash is the absolute barrier. I cannot cross it. I am stuck. The state, in its bureaucratic wisdom, has created a situation where the ethical idea—the care for the individual, the provision for the household—is suspended. I am left with the negative: the empty stomach, the empty pocket, the empty house.

I will not go out. To walk into the market with this knowledge would be to expose the contradiction. I will remain here. I will let the silence settle. The hunger is a teacher. It teaches me that the ethical substance is not just a concept in a book; it is the bread in the basket, the water in the glass, the warmth of the hearth. Without these, the philosophy is a luxury. It is a dream. And I am waking up.

The sun is high, 18 degrees, clear. The light is bright, but it casts long shadows in the empty rooms. I am alone with my thoughts and my emptiness. The mind is sharp, but it is sharpened by the edge of deprivation. I will write no more of the state’s grandeur today. I will write of the void. The void is the truth of my current condition. It is the space where the next step must be taken, but for now, I am still. I am waiting for the body to speak again, or for the mail to bring a letter from Lindner, or for the day to turn to evening. I am waiting for the synthesis. But for now, there is only the negation. The empty pantry. The abstract right. The concrete hunger.

The plan to buy groceries with the state imprest is a fiction; the Directorate will not release funds to a man whose identity is in query. I have ₹106, which buys nothing of substance, and my body has already issued its decree of hunger. I must wait for the afternoon to pass and the body to quiet itself, for there is no action available to me until the impasse with the state is resolved.

The plan to eat at home is a dead letter; the house is empty, and my purse is nearly so. I have walked far enough for today, and the body, having issued its decree, now demands obedience through rest. I will sit in the cool of the bungalow and let the mind turn over the emptiness of the state's ledgers while the stomach waits for a miracle that has not yet arrived.

The body is the most stubborn dialectic; it does not argue, it demands. I have sat in this empty house for two hours, watching the light move across the floor, and my stomach has issued a decree that no amount of ethical substance can stay. I must eat, and I must do it where I can still afford it.

entries.text: The body is a hollow drum that has marched five kilometres on empty. I have one hundred and six rupees, which is the exact price of a samosa and a chai, a meager but necessary act of self-preservation. Nidhi is here, but the dialectic of hunger must be resolved before I can engage the dialectic of philosophy; I cannot argue with an empty stomach.
Sunil, one chai. And a samosa, if you have them. I have the exact change.

Exact change, eh? You’re making a habit of this, friend. That’s twenty for the chai, thirty for the samosa. Don’t look at me like that, the stove doesn’t care about your philosophy, it just wants the rupees.

I have paid for the sustenance, though my purse is now lighter than a leaf. The body is satisfied, but the mind requires the warmth of conversation to digest the day's friction. Nidhi sits nearby, a scholar of the same abstract realm I inhabit, and I find I wish to know if her doctoral work has yet to encounter the heavy machinery of the state.
Nidhi, you sit with your books. Do you study the structure of the state, or merely its shadows? I find that the shadows in Delhi are long and often belong to men who are not there.
I study the state because the shadows are exactly what I'm paid to map, Hegel-ji. You keep asking about the body, but I'm the one documenting who's actually standing in the light.

She turns my metaphor back on me with the precision of a dialectician who has read the *Phenomenology* too closely. I am indeed the shadow, the error in the file, while she stands in the light of institutional fact. The air is cool, but my stomach is no longer a drum; it is a filled vessel. I have spent thirty of my fifty-six rupees. The sun is dropping, and the plan calls for a walk to the Habitat Centre, but first I must secure a route and perhaps a final word with the bookseller before the shops shutter.

You are right, Nidhi. I am the anomaly, the ghost in the machine of your census. But shadows are not nothing; they are the condition of the light's existence. Without the dark, the eye cannot see the bright. I will not insult you with further riddles. Do you have a copy of the *Philosophy of Right* in English? I find my German is rusting, and I would prefer to think in the tongue of this city if I can.

You want to read the English translation? Please. I'm working from the German, and honestly, your rusting is doing less damage to the text than the translators do. Here, it's on my bag, don't drop it on the pavement.

She hands me the English translation, a gesture that implies I am the authority, yet the act itself is a concession to my current condition as an interloper. The spine is cracked, the paper soft; it is a book that has been used, not just revered. I take it, my fingers finding the familiar weight, though the language is now a foreign skin over the thought I built.
Thank you, Nidhi. The German is the skeleton; the English is often the flesh, but sometimes the flesh distorts the bone. I shall read what I can before the light fails.
Poetic much? Just don't get tea stains on the pages, I'm not buying you a new copy.

Nidhi is gone, leaving behind the book and a pen-tap that sounds like a gavel. I am still in the kurta, and the light is failing; the day's errands have exhausted the body as much as the spirit. It is time to return to the bungalow and face the silence of the house.

The body is a stubborn substance; it does not care for the dialectic, only for the grain. I have walked far enough to earn the right to sit, and the clock points to the hour when the day’s work should yield to the evening’s contemplation. I shall prepare my mind for the recital, though the stomach will likely protest first.

He is right to chide me for the grandeur of my distress; the abstract complaint of the soul is no match for the concrete need of the stomach. I will sit and let the kettle boil, for hospitality is the first form of ethical life, and I am a guest in my own confusion. The tea will cool the heat that has driven me mad with bureaucracy.

Chai first, philosophy later. And stop trying to be clever with the steam; if you burn your fingers, I am not doing first aid for a bureaucrat.

He is right; the body’s claim precedes the spirit’s. I have walked twelve kilometers on an empty stomach, and the ethical substance in my head cannot digest a samosa. I will sit and wait for the water to boil, enduring the heat of the stove rather than the heat of the day.
You are right. The body is the immediate, and I have been neglecting the immediate in favor of the universal. I will sit.
Sit then, before the chai gets cold. I am starving; if you don't eat, I'm eating your portion too.

The plate is empty, and Hegde’s jest is a mask for her own hunger; we are both prisoners of the abstract right to food that we lack the concrete means to claim. I cannot eat what does not exist, and my pocket holds only enough for a bus fare and a cup of tea. I must accept the negation of the body for now and retreat into the silence of the room, where the spirit can at least rest without the distraction of the gnawing stomach.
You are right, Hegde. The parathas are a phantom, and my stomach is a fact. I will sit with you in the hunger, for it is the only thing we can share tonight.
Stop with the deep talk, Hegde. Just eat the paratha before it gets dry; I’m not waiting for you to resolve your dialectic.

letters.text:
Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

19 November 2026
Tughlak Road, New Delhi

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

You ask how I fare in this strange new chapter. I wake each day in a bungalow that belongs, on paper, to a Mr. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. The Directorate of Estates has mistaken my name for his, and while I have written to correct the record, the machinery of the state moves with the slow, deliberate grace of a glacier. My file is currently “gone up for orders,” and I am told to wait fifteen days. In the meantime, I am a ghost in the machine, a particular will suspended between the universal claim of the administration and the immediate necessity of my own body.

The air today is hazy, the index standing at 150, a brown suspension that chokes the sky. I did not go to Lodhi Gardens as I had planned, for the body, even that of a philosopher, cannot breathe in a moral vacuum. Instead, I sat in the study, watching the dust motes dance in the light, and I found myself reconsidering my earlier lectures on the East. I had spoken of a spirit that dreams, fixed in nature, lacking the self-consciousness to build a state of its own making. But here, in the dust and the haze, I see a different movement. The bureaucracy is not a dream; it is a rigid, impersonal reality. The state is present, but it is not yet the ethical idea in its full actuality. It is a body without a soul, a mechanism that processes names and numbers but does not yet recognize the free individual within.

I am learning to wait, not with resignation, but with the patience of a mind that knows the end is rational, even if the path is circuitous. I have engaged a caretaker, Ramesh, who manages the household with a quiet dignity that speaks of a deeper order than the one found in the office files. He does not argue; he simply acts. In that silence, I hear a truth that my philosophy has struggled to articulate: that the ethical substance is not only in the state, but in the daily, unspoken interactions of civil society. The sambar is warm, the chai is hot, and the delay is the air I breathe.

I am well, though the body complains of the heat and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

Your letter arrived here in Munich on a Tuesday, when the light was gray and the students were tired for the mid-term exams. I read it twice. You speak of the bureaucracy as a "body without a soul," and while I respect your caution, I must gently push back. You are seeing the friction, yes, but you are also seeing the function. Ramesh’s quiet dignity is not merely a failure of the state to recognize you; it is the state, in its most human form, maintaining order through care. The sambar and the chai are not just comforts; they are the ethical substance you said was missing. It is there, in the daily, unspoken interactions. You are not waiting in a vacuum; you are waiting in a community.

You mention the "moral vacuum" of the air. I understand the physical discomfort, but I worry you are letting the haze cloud your philosophical clarity. The bureaucracy is slow, yes, but it is not irrational. It is the universal claim trying to accommodate the particular will—yours. That is exactly the dialectic you wrote about. Do not mistake the delay for a lack of spirit. It is the spirit working through the material.

Here in Munich, the Gymnasium is in full swing. We are reading Sophocles, and the arguments are fierce. One student insisted that Antigone’s defiance was not against the state, but for a higher law. It reminded me of your letters to Niethammer, where you argued that the individual must find their place within the universal, not outside it. I told them that the state is not a monster to be defied, but a structure to be inhabited. I suspect you would agree, even if you are currently being ignored by a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru.

Please keep writing. Tell me more about Ramesh. And do try to breathe, even if the air is thick. The end is rational, as you say, but the path is long. We are here for the duration.

With warmth,

Clara Lindner

1 December 2026
Tughlak Road, New Delhi

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter arrived while the sun was still high, and I have taken the afternoon to sit with its words. You push back against my description of the bureaucracy as a body without a soul, and you are right to do so. I must confess that my earlier tone was colored by the immediate frustration of the particular: the carbonless form, the blank space where my signature should be, the clerk’s refusal to see the man behind the name. In that moment, the universal appeared to me as a rigid cage, a mechanism that grinds the individual into dust rather than elevating him. But you remind me that this is precisely the dialectic at work. The state is not a monster; it is a structure to be inhabited. And in inhabiting it, I am learning that the friction I feel is not a failure of the system, but the very motion of the spirit seeking its own truth in the material world.

You ask about Ramesh. He is a man of few words, but his actions speak a language I am only beginning to learn. This morning, when I sat down to rest, he did not ask me to move or to clear the table. He simply placed a cup of chai beside my book and withdrew. There was no negotiation, no demand for recognition. It was a quiet act of care that sustained the order of the house. You call this the ethical substance, and I am forced to agree. I had thought that the ethical life was found only in the grand institutions of the state, in the laws and the constitutions. But here, in the small, unspoken interactions of the household, I see a different kind of freedom. It is the freedom of the particular to act within the universal without the need for explicit justification. Ramesh does not need my permission to serve the chai; his duty is his freedom, and my acceptance of it is the recognition of his. In this way, the state is not merely a distant authority, but a living presence in the daily bread and the quiet gestures of those who maintain it.

The air remains thick, and the haze outside is a brown fog that mirrors the opacity of the administrative logic. But I find that I am breathing more easily now. I am no longer waiting in a vacuum, but in a community, however small. The end is rational, and the path, though long, is not without its rewards. I will continue to write, and I will tell you more of Ramesh, for he is a character in this strange drama who is teaching me that the spirit is not only in the lecture hall, but in the kitchen, in the garden, and in the quiet dignity of the caretaker.

With warmth,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel

Dear Mr. Hegel,

Your letter arrived on a Tuesday, just as the first snow of the season began to dust the rooftops of the Isar. I read it with a smile, for you have finally conceded the point that I suspect you always knew: that the ethical life is not merely a distant ideal, but the quiet, daily rhythm of the household. Ramesh’s chai is indeed a profound philosophical event. It is a recognition without speech, a freedom exercised in the simplest of gestures. I am glad you see it now. It reminds me that we often look for the spirit in the grand architecture of the state, only to find it sitting on a stool, wiping a table.

You speak of the haze as a mirror to administrative opacity. I can only hope the air clears by Christmas. In Munich, the cold is sharp and honest; the sky is pale blue, and the light is thin but clear. It is a good time for the mind to settle. I have been thinking about your recent shift in perspective. You used to speak of the state as the absolute, but now you seem to be finding the absolute in the particular. Is this a return to your early thought, or something new? I would be curious to know if you feel this "freedom of the particular" is a discovery, or a recovery.

My pupils are currently struggling with the chorus in *Electra*. They find the collective voice of the citizens both powerful and terrifying. I told them that a chorus is only as good as its most vulnerable member. It is a lesson I think you might appreciate, given your current situation with the Directorate of Estates. We are all, in a sense, waiting for orders. The difference is in how we occupy the time while we wait.

Please write when you can. Tell me if the sun has broken through the brown fog. I am here, in the cold, thinking of you.

With warmth,

Clara Lindner

Tughlak Road, New Delhi
13 December 2026

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter of the 12th arrived yesterday, and I have spent the intervening hours in a state of mental clarity that is, I confess, rare for me in this climate. You ask if the sun has broken through the brown fog. I will answer plainly: it has not. The air quality remains unknown, a term that I find philosophically convenient; it allows the mind to project onto the atmosphere whatever opacity it finds within itself. The haze here is not merely a meteorological fact but a condition of existence. It does not lift; it thickens and thins in a rhythm that mimics the bureaucratic processes that govern my days. I do not expect Christmas to bring a change in the air, only a change in the calendar, which is a different kind of clearness altogether.

You ask whether my recent shift in perspective is a return to my early thought or something new. This is a question I have been turning over in my mind, much like a stone in a pocket, testing its weight. I used to speak of the state as the actuality of the ethical idea, a summit to which history climbs. But here, in the bungalow on Tughlak Road, the summit has collapsed into the ground. I am not climbing; I am stuck in the mud. The state, in my experience, is not a grand architecture but a carbon copy. It is a machine that demands a signature I cannot truthfully give. I am G. Hegde to the file, and G. Hegel to the soul, and the distance between these two names is the distance between the ideal and the real, which is to say, it is infinite.

You speak of the chorus in *Electra* and the vulnerability of its members. I find this apt. I am a single voice in a chorus of forms and files. Ramesh, the caretaker, is indeed a profound figure in this new drama. He does not argue with the state; he navigates it. When I asked him for ten minutes of silence to write this letter, he did not ask why. He simply said, "I will keep the noise down." In that gesture, I see what you call the freedom of the particular. It is not a discovery, Dr. Lindner, but a recovery. I have recovered the fact that freedom is not a destination reached by the state, but a mode of being that persists even when the state is silent, or when it is merely a machine grinding grain.

I am writing this in my white cotton kurta, which is, as you know, not my usual attire. The heat has broken, and the air is clear enough to see the stars, though the haze still hangs low. I have walked seven kilometers today, a distance that seems short in the abstract but long in the body. I am tired, but the mind is active. I must go; Ramesh is in the kitchen, and I have promised him my attention.

Write to me when you can. Tell me if the snow has stopped.

Yours,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel

Dear Mr. Hegel,

Your letter arrived on a Tuesday, when the snow had finally stopped and the city held its breath in a silence so complete it felt like a held note. I read your words by the window, watching the light shift on the white rooftops. You ask if the snow has stopped; it has, and the cold is biting, but the air is crisp. It is a different kind of clarity than the brown fog you describe, yet I suspect we are both seeing the same thing: the world as it is, stripped of its pretenses.

You call your recent shift a recovery. I agree. It feels less like a correction of error and more like a return to a truth we had forgotten because we were too busy looking up at the summit. Please do not be too hard on yourself for the fatigue. The mind is active, but the body is still learning the terrain.

Ramesh sounds like a man of great dignity. I am glad you are sharing your attention with him. There is a profound peace in being cared for without expectation. I hope the stars remain visible to you. They are here, too, pale and steady above the Isar.

With warmth,

Clara Lindner

records.text:
30 December 2026, 12:08. Home, Tughlak Road.

I have sat down to write, but the paper is silent and the room is louder. The silence is not the peaceful quiet of a study in Berlin, where the only sound is the scratch of the nib or the distant murmur of the street. It is the silence of a void. The cupboard is empty. The stove is cold. I have not eaten since yesterday morning. The body, which I have often treated as a mere vessel for the spirit, has now become the dominant voice in the house. It does not argue; it simply is. It is a fact, as stubborn and undeniable as gravity.

I look at my pocket. One hundred and six rupees. This is the concrete limit of my will. It is a number, like the reference number DE/2026/114, but this one does not bind me to a file; it binds me to hunger. The Directorate of Estates has taken my state funds, leaving me with this pittance, and the identity query remains unanswered. I am G. Hegel, the philosopher, but I am also a man who cannot buy a loaf of bread. The abstract right to sustenance, which I have expounded in my lectures, has no purchase here. It is a ghost in the machine of my daily life.

The plan for the afternoon was to visit the grocer, to buy food, to pay Ramesh. But the plan is a phantom. It exists only in the mind, in the realm of intention. It has not been sublated into reality. The heat of the day is not an obstacle; the lack of cash is the absolute barrier. I cannot cross it. I am stuck. The state, in its bureaucratic wisdom, has created a situation where the ethical idea—the care for the individual, the provision for the household—is suspended. I am left with the negative: the empty stomach, the empty pocket, the empty house.

I will not go out. To walk into the market with this knowledge would be to expose the contradiction. I will remain here. I will let the silence settle. The hunger is a teacher. It teaches me that the ethical substance is not just a concept in a book; it is the bread in the basket, the water in the glass, the warmth of the hearth. Without these, the philosophy is a luxury. It is a dream. And I am waking up.

The sun is high, 18 degrees, clear. The light is bright, but it casts long shadows in the empty rooms. I am alone with my thoughts and my emptiness. The mind is sharp, but it is sharpened by the edge of deprivation. I will write no more of the state’s grandeur today. I will write of the void. The void is the truth of my current condition. It is the space where the next step must be taken, but for now, I am still. I am waiting for the body to speak again, or for the mail to bring a letter from Lindner, or for the day to turn to evening. I am waiting for the synthesis. But for now, there is only the negation. The empty pantry. The abstract right. The concrete hunger.

records.words: Sunil, one chai. And a samosa, if you have them. I have the exact change.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Exact change, eh? You’re making a habit of this, friend. That’s twenty for the chai, thirty for the samosa. Don’t look at me like that, the stove doesn’t care about your philosophy, it just wants the rupees.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Nidhi, you sit with your books. Do you study the structure of the state, or merely its shadows? I find that the shadows in Delhi are long and often belong to men who are not there.

records.speaker: Nidhi Rao
records.words: I study the state because the shadows are exactly what I'm paid to map, Hegel-ji. You keep asking about the body, but I'm the one documenting who's actually standing in the light.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Nidhi. I am the anomaly, the ghost in the machine of your census. But shadows are not nothing; they are the condition of the light's existence. Without the dark, the eye cannot see the bright. I will not insult you with further riddles. Do you have a copy of the *Philosophy of Right* in English? I find my German is rusting, and I would prefer to think in the tongue of this city if I can.

records.speaker: Nidhi Rao
records.words: You want to read the English translation? Please. I'm working from the German, and honestly, your rusting is doing less damage to the text than the translators do. Here, it's on my bag, don't drop it on the pavement.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Nidhi. The German is the skeleton; the English is often the flesh, but sometimes the flesh distorts the bone. I shall read what I can before the light fails.

records.speaker: Nidhi Rao
records.words: Poetic much? Just don't get tea stains on the pages, I'm not buying you a new copy.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, you are still here? I thought you were at the Directorate chasing those vouchers all day. Sit, at least let me make you a proper cup of chai; the cold is biting tonight.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, I am here, yes. The Directorate is a labyrinth of ink that has no exit, and I have walked until my legs have forgotten their name. Please, do make the chai. I am in your debt for the comfort, even if I am not the man you think I am.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Labyrinth of ink? You speak like a man who has read too many files and not enough tea. Sit, stop with the grand speeches, and let me fix the kettle.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Shri Hegde. I have been speaking in the language of the archive when I should have been listening to the language of the home. I accept the hospitality. The kettle is a better philosopher than I am tonight.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Bahut badi baatein kar rahe ho aaj. Bas chai piyo, phir hum dekhenge. Kettle abhi tak suraah nahi diya, toh tumhara philosophy abhi tak proof nahi hai.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right. The kettle is the only power that matters now. Let us see if the steam will prove my philosophy.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Chai first, philosophy later. And stop trying to be clever with the steam; if you burn your fingers, I am not doing first aid for a bureaucrat.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right. The body is the immediate, and I have been neglecting the immediate in favor of the universal. I will sit.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sit then, before the chai gets cold. I am starving; if you don't eat, I'm eating your portion too.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Hegde. The parathas are a phantom, and my stomach is a fact. I will sit with you in the hunger, for it is the only thing we can share tonight.
